content:
Touma woke to find Mio standing in the corner.

Not her voice. Not the familiar pressure of her presence, or a private comment arriving before he had finished forming the thought that prompted it.

Mio herself.

He stared.

She glanced away from the door long enough to notice. “What?”

“You’re there.”

“Yes.”

“You can’t just be there.”

“Where would you prefer?”

That was not the part he meant, and she knew it.

Above him, the ceiling was a suspicious beige. The broken lamp still stood beside the futon. The carpet still smelled of dust, instant coffee, and cheap disinfectant. Nothing about the safehouse had improved overnight. It was still a room rented by someone who had apparently considered cleanliness a matter of keeping the stains small.

But now Mio stood in its corner like a clerical error large enough to become visible.

She was looking around again. Not with curiosity, exactly. Her gaze moved from the window to the kitchenette counter, then back to the door, as if the room might have teeth it had not yet shown her.

“Stop staring,” she said.

“I’m checking something.”

“What?”

“Whether you disappear when I blink.”

“Have I?”

“No.”

“Then you can stop checking.”

His face grew hot.

Until now, there had been a layer between the strange thing happening to him and the rest of the world. Thin, unreliable, but there. A voice only he could hear could still be filed under private problems. He could pretend to be thinking. He could refrain from answering aloud. He could endure a clerk looking at him strangely and leave before the situation acquired witnesses.

There was no useful category for a girl standing in his bedroom who had not been there when he went to sleep.

Or who had been there, but not like this.

He sat up. Mio shifted closer, watching him with an expression he could now see rather than infer.

That was another problem.

He reached to pull the blanket off his legs.

His hand went through her knee.

Touma stopped.

There had been no resistance. His hand had simply occupied a place where, by every rule his eyes understood, it should not have been able to go.

Mio jerked back. The movement had a slight delay to it, as though the intention had arrived before the rest of her.

“Warn me before you do that.”

“I didn’t mean to.”

“That’s what makes it worse.”

He withdrew his hand carefully. There was no reason to be careful now. His body insisted anyway.

“Can you feel anything?”

She looked at him.

“Physically or emotionally?”

“I meant—”

“I know what you meant. It was a broad question.”

“Could you not act like a person who understands me too well for one minute?”

“That was always the case.”

He looked down at the blanket.

She had a point. That did not make any of this easier.

The previous night returned in pieces: instructions, the limiter, Nico speaking with the careful precision of someone who needed each word to remain true. Touma remembered enough to know this had not happened without warning. He did not remember anything that adequately explained waking up to it.

Mio moved her hand, then let it fall again. There was that slight lag, the impression of a thought asking the room for permission before becoming motion.

He had heard her hesitate before. He had heard irritation, uncertainty, the changes in her voice when she was trying not to tell him something.

This was different.

Her shoulders tightened when something sounded beyond the door. She drew a breath before answering a question that did not seem to require one. She kept deciding where to put her hands.

She seemed more alive than she had when she was only audible, and he disliked the implication that she had needed to become visible for him to notice.

He could see her fear now.

That was what finally made him look away.

Touma got off the futon and began pacing the narrow strip of carpet between it and the kitchenette. There was barely enough room for three steps before he had to turn.

Mio watched him.

He reached the counter, turned, and glanced at her.

Reached the futon, turned, and glanced at her again.

“Is that helping?” she asked.

“No.”

“Then why are you doing it?”

He stopped.

Because standing still meant having to decide where to stand in relation to her. Because his body kept treating her as the center of the room. Because being watched by her had somehow become a physical experience, even though she had been watching him before.

None of those sounded like things he could say.

“I’m thinking.”

“You can do that sitting down.”

“Apparently not.”

This was not a tactical problem. He almost wished it were. He knew how to worry about exits, pursuit, the wrong person recognizing his face.

He did not know where to look while an impossible girl stood beside his bed, offended by him and frightened of the same room he was trying to get used to.

The door opened.

Touma turned so quickly he nearly struck the counter.

Nico stopped in the doorway.

Her gaze went to him, then to Mio. It remained there a fraction too long before she brought it back.

“You’re both awake.”

Touma stared at her. “You knew she could do that?”

“No.”

Too fast.

Nico seemed to hear it too. She adjusted her grip on the door handle.

“Not this. Not with any certainty.”

“That’s a different answer.”

“It’s a more precise answer.”

Mio folded her arms. Or began to, hesitated, then completed the movement.

Nico watched despite herself.

For a moment, Touma saw the problem plainly: whatever Nico had expected to examine was no longer confined to a closed system. It stood across the room and listened to her explanations. It could object.

Then the doorway caught his attention.

The rule about witnesses had not gone away just because he had been too embarrassed to think about it. Nico was still standing where someone passing outside might see around her.

“Close the door,” he said.

She did, immediately.

The click made the room feel smaller.

“The limiter is stable for the moment,” Nico said. “The projection isn’t.”

“Projection,” Touma repeated.

“Yes.”

“You make it sound like something for a school presentation.”

“I’m trying to distinguish what we know from what we don’t.”

“Then distinguish it without making me sound like equipment,” Mio said.

Nico’s mouth tightened.

“The visible manifestation may be a side effect.”

“A side effect,” Touma said.

“That isn’t a judgment. It describes the relationship between the procedure and the result.”

“The result is standing right there.”

“I can see that.”

It came out sharper than her previous answers. Nico took a breath and tried again.

“I can see her. That is part of the problem.”

Mio looked between them. “Could you both stop arguing about which words make this less alarming?”

Touma turned to her. “You’re taking her side?”

“I’m taking the side where we continue existing.”

Nico gave a small, unsteady nod, as though grateful for the agreement but not at all reassured by its source.

Touma leaned against the counter. Everything about this morning seemed to be arriving through a bad signal. Words he understood kept connecting to meanings he did not want. The rules felt like passwords that changed while he was typing them.

“All right,” he said. “What does unstable mean?”

“It means I can’t tell you how long this will last. Or establish the limits from what we’ve seen so far.”

“Can you turn it off?”

“I don’t know.”

Mio went still.

He saw it. Nico saw it too.

Neither of them tried to make the answer sound better.

“There’s something more immediate,” Nico said.

Touma looked at her.

“If I can register her presence outside the original arrangement, other systems may be able to register it too.”

He glanced at Mio before he could stop himself.

“What systems?”

“Cameras. Biometrics. Active recognition filters.”

The room seemed to lose the protection of its walls.

He thought of the route here. The entrance. The clerk. All the places where being unremarkable had mattered, where he had relied on the difference between what was happening to him and what anyone else could see.

“And people?” he asked.

“Possibly. We don’t know how broadly this extends.”

“But you can see her.”

“Yes.”

“So can I.”

“Yes.”

Mio looked toward the closed door.

Touma had spent the first minutes of the morning wishing he could stop looking at her. Now he was trying to imagine every device between this room and the street doing the same thing—and keeping a record.

“That bad?” he asked.

Nico’s eyes flicked to Mio, then back to him.

“Bad enough for you.”
